o: A server table that stores HTML submitted by users
Client code that handles outside data in a dangerous way
A browser add-on that blocks scripts from running
A CSS rule that hides risky nodes from the page
questions.x: A sink is where data flows into something that can change what the browser parses or runs. innerHTML, eval, and location assignments are common examples. A DOM XSS bug is usually a source connected to a sink.
questions.h: Sink means data flows into something. Which client operations can turn outside data into HTML or code the browser will run?

questions.q: When is a DOM XSS bug present?
o: When attacker data from a source reaches a sink
Whenever a page assigns innerHTML at least once
Whenever a URL contains any query parameter
When the server stores comments in a database
questions.x: A source is where data enters the page. A sink is where that data is handled dangerously. Neither alone is the bug. DOM XSS appears when attacker-controlled data flows from a source into a sink.
questions.h: Think of water from a tap into a drain. Which pairing actually creates the XSS bug?

questions.q: How do innerHTML and textContent treat a string that contains HTML tags?
o: Both parse the string as HTML and build new nodes
innerHTML parses HTML while textContent keeps it as text
Both treat the string as plain text on the page
textContent parses HTML while innerHTML keeps it as text
questions.x: innerHTML runs the HTML parser, so tags and attributes can become real nodes and handlers. textContent and innerText treat the value as plain text, so a script tag stays visible characters on screen.
questions.h: One of these properties assigns text without running the HTML parser on the value.

questions.q: Which assignment is a classic HTML sink?
o: node.textContent = attackerString
node.innerHTML = attackerString
node.innerText = attackerString
node.dataset.note = attackerString
questions.x: Assigning to innerHTML (also outerHTML, insertAdjacentHTML, and document.write) parses markup. textContent and innerText do not. A payload like an img with onerror can become a real element only if the parser runs.
questions.h: Which write operation turns a string into parsed HTML nodes rather than literal text?

questions.q: What separates reflected DOM XSS from ordinary reflected XSS?
o: DOM XSS needs stored data, ordinary XSS does not need it
DOM XSS only works in Firefox, never in Chromium browsers
DOM XSS reads the payload in client script, not from page HTML
Ordinary XSS uses innerHTML while DOM XSS uses eval only
questions.x: Ordinary reflected XSS already has the payload in the server HTML. Reflected DOM XSS can have a clean page source while client script reads a URL parameter and writes it to a sink such as innerHTML.
questions.h: In one bug the payload is in the page source. In DOM XSS, who reads the payload and who writes it?
